content.overview: Administrative tribunals were created to provide specialised, relatively speedy and less formal adjudication of disputes arising from the expansion of the administrative state. Their advantages must be weighed against independence, expertise and residual High Court review under L. Chandra Kumar.
content.glance: List the claimed advantages (specialisation, speed, flexibility, cost, expertise); note the constitutional constraints on independence and review; apply to the tribunal under consideration.
content.study: The growth of the welfare and regulatory state produced a volume of disputes that ordinary courts could not absorb efficiently. Tribunals offer subject-matter expertise, flexible procedure, and potentially faster disposal. These advantages are legitimate only when the tribunal is independent, its members are properly qualified, and its decisions remain subject to High Court judicial review under Articles 226/227. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in Articles 323A/323B and the parent tribunal statute. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of this doctrine.

sections.heading: Specialisation and Expertise
sections.body: Tribunals can combine judicial and technical members, improving fact-finding in specialised fields.

sections.heading: Speed and Flexibility
sections.body: Less formal procedure and focused jurisdiction can reduce delay relative to ordinary civil process.

sections.heading: Cost and Accessibility
sections.body: Lower procedural formality may reduce cost and improve access for affected persons.

sections.heading: Constitutional Limits
sections.body: Advantages cannot justify dilution of independence or exclusion of High Court review (L. Chandra Kumar).

sections.heading: Balancing Rationale
sections.body: The case for tribunals rests on efficiency plus fairness; efficiency alone is not a sufficient justification.

examples.title: Specialised membership
examples.body: A tax tribunal includes members with accountancy and judicial experience. The mixed composition is an advantage only if independence and fair procedure are secured.

examples.title: Speed without fairness
examples.body: A tribunal disposes of cases rapidly by denying notice and hearing. Speed is not a legitimate advantage when it destroys natural justice.

hypotheticals.question: Do tribunal advantages justify ousting High Court review?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. L. Chandra Kumar holds that High Court judicial review under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure and cannot be ousted.

hypotheticals.question: Is expertise a substitute for legal independence?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Expertise aids fact-finding; independence and impartiality remain constitutional requirements.

distinctions.title: Tribunal advantages vs ordinary court process
distinctions.right: General jurisdiction, formal procedure, full judicial independence

misconceptions.trap: Tribunals are always faster and therefore always preferable.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is an advantage only when fairness and independence are preserved.
High Court review cannot be ousted; advantages operate within the constitutional framework.

cases.name: L. Chandra Kumar v Union of India
cases.issue: Whether tribunal decisions can exclude High Court judicial review.
cases.ratioDecidendi: High Court judicial review under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure; tribunals are subject to that supervision.
cases.holding: Tribunal model affirmed subject to constitutional supervision.
cases.relevance: Authority already in related tribunal files.

cases.name: Union of India v Madras Bar Association
cases.issue: What institutional features are constitutionally necessary?
cases.ratioDecidendi: Independence, impartiality, proper qualifications and secure conditions are central to valid tribunal design.
cases.holding: Defective aspects of the framework invalidated.
cases.relevance: Authority already in related tribunal files.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a tribunals-advantages problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. List claimed advantages. II. Test independence and fairness conditions. III. Note residual High Court review. IV. Conclude whether the advantage is legitimate on the facts.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Advantages identified; independence analysis; review residual; precise relief.

examTips: List five advantages and one constitutional limit.
Never treat speed as justifying denial of natural justice.
Cite L. Chandra Kumar for the review residual.
